newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gore visit to Japan seen as mainly symbolic.
newsitem.headline: Gore visit to Japan seen as mainly symbolic.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore visits Japan this weekend on a mainly symbolic visit to show that ties between the two nations remain the cornerstone of American policy in Asia.

Gore arrives in Tokyo on Sunday afternoon and spends just 24 hours in Japan before flying on to Beijing and then Seoul in the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to the region since President Bill Clinton started his second term.

Japanese officials said there was no "specific agenda" for the visit and went out of their way to play down speculation it was linked to a controversy about the future of U.S. military bases on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa.
"There are no indications that Mr. Gore will dwell on the Okinawa issue." a senior Japanese official said.

About 3,000 Okinawans who own land covering 362,000 sq metres (433,000 sq yards) on 12 bases including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base are refusing to renew leases when they expire on May 15.
About 75 percent of U.S. bases in Japan are on Okinawa, which makes up less than one percent of Japanese territory.
Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015, an action Tokyo strongly opposes.
In a politically risky move, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is considering legislation to expropriate the land.
However the legislation could cost him the support of the loose alliance of parties which allows Hashimoto's minority government to rule.
Gore's visit is just part of a flurry of diplomatic activity between Washington and Tokyo in the first months of Clinton's new administration.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has already visited Tokyo and in the next month Defence Secretary William Cohen and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin are also due to visit.
At the end of April Hashimoto also travels to Washington for a meeting with Clinton.

"U.S. leaders, including Clinton and Albright, have time and again said the United States places priority on Asia and we understand Mr. Gore's visit in this light," the foreign ministry official said.
He said key foreign policy subjects likely to be discussed between Gore and Hashimoto were North Korea and China.
With trade wars between the two nations for the moment a thing of the past, Gore is also likely to reassure Hashimoto that Washington does not take its ties with Japan for granted.
There has been speculation in some Japanese media that China was now the United States' top priority in Asia, a view disputed by U.S. officials.
"Japan is, and always will be, a cornerstone of our Asian policy," a U.S. official said.
Gore arrives in a week when a Japanese newspaper survey found a record number of Americans and Japanese believe bilateral relations were good.

The survey by the Yomiuri Shimbun and Gallup Organisation said 46 percent of both Japanese and Americans felt ties were good, a 23 percentage point rise among Japanese and 18 percentage point rise among Americans from a 1995 survey.
The Yomiuri said the absence of trade rows and a shared view by Americans and Japanese that China could one day pose a security threat appeared to be the main reasons for the rise.
